items.title: Multimodal RAG over Slides and Video
items.abstract:
Multimodal RAG over Slides and Video was recorded as a Main Track session at the 2026 AI Engineering Summit. The session focuses on models that combine vision, language, and structured interfaces. The project referenced by this session is LLaVA-VL/LLaVA-NeXT. Programme notes describe the project as: the open-source LLaVA-NeXT project, which the speaker uses as the reference implementation for the techniques shown on stage. The speaker combines architecture diagrams, production anecdotes, and benchmark results, and reserves time at the end for questions from practitioners.

The closing section lists open problems in multimodal agents that must read, point, and act in the same environment.

The talk demonstrates human review loops that catch hallucinated chart values before model output reaches an executive dashboard.

The speaker compares captioning, grounding, and instruction-following objectives, noting that each objective produces different failure patterns.

Evaluation receives substantial attention, because multimodal benchmarks are easy to overfit and hard to reproduce across preprocessing pipelines.

Serving considerations include image preprocessing latency, cache keys for repeated media, and safe fallbacks when vision input is malformed.

Document understanding examples show why resolution, layout, and reading order matter more than raw parameter count for business documents.

Method and measurement. The team used a staged rollout with canary traffic, automatic rollback, and a weekly review of quality regressions. A cost table compares tokens, latency, engineering hours, and operational risk for each option discussed. The methodology section walks through the baseline, the instrumentation used to measure it, and the conditions under which the improvement appears. Each experiment reports hardware, batch sizes, prompt templates, and evaluation settings so the audience can judge how far the result will transfer.

Takeaways. The team encourages readers to treat every generated artifact as untrusted until verified by a deterministic check. A second takeaway is that observability and evaluation must be designed together with the feature. The session ends with a short reading list and an invitation to contribute issues and reproduction scripts to the referenced project. The final advice is to document the assumptions behind a benchmark, because those assumptions are what future maintainers will question.

Session context. The room was full, and the questions after the talk focused on deployment details rather than demos. Slides, recordings, and short notes accompany the session in the archive. The presentation assumes familiarity with Python and basic model-serving concepts but does not require research experience.

Several recommendations were framed as defaults that teams can start with and then relax only after measuring the tradeoff in their own environment.

The presenter noted that documentation quality often determines whether a technique is adopted, since most teams first encounter the idea through an internal write-up rather than the original paper.

The presentation closed with an open invitation to reproduce the benchmark and report divergence, since negative results are also useful.

A follow-up workshop covers the hands-on version of the same material, with exercises that rebuild a small end-to-end pipeline.

The talk included a short retrospective on what the team would do differently if they started again with the same constraints.

The session included a brief discussion of privacy, including how long traces are retained and how user data is scrubbed before storage.

A comparison slide showed the same workload before and after the change, with percentile latencies rather than averages so that tail behavior was visible.

During the audience discussion, one participant described a similar rollout that stalled because ownership was split across teams; the speaker recommended a single service owner for the end-to-end workflow.

The presenter emphasized that tooling should make the safe path the easy path, because operators under pressure tend to take shortcuts.

The speaker answered a question about security by describing the permission model, the sandbox boundary, and the review process for sensitive actions.

Audience questions ranged from hardware selection to team structure, and the answers consistently returned to clarity of measurement.

The speaker drew a distinction between a demo that succeeds once and a system that succeeds repeatedly under noisy inputs.

items.title: Quantization Recipes That Actually Ship
items.abstract:
Quantization Recipes That Actually Ship was recorded as a Lightning Talk session at the 2026 AI Engineering Summit. The session focuses on serving and optimizing large models under real production constraints. The project referenced by this session is huggingface/transformers. Programme notes describe the project as: the open-source transformers project, which the speaker uses as the reference implementation for the techniques shown on stage. The speaker combines architecture diagrams, production anecdotes, and benchmark results, and reserves time at the end for questions from practitioners.

Benchmarks are reported at the request level, with percentile latency, throughput under saturation, and memory headroom so that operators can reproduce the result.

Continuous batching and paged attention are explained through production traces rather than benchmark charts, including the tail latency effects that appear when long and short requests mix.

Quantization is presented as a pipeline rather than a single switch: calibration, outlier handling, kernel support, and accuracy regression checks all matter.

A detailed section covers cache reuse, prefix sharing, and eviction policies, with guidance on when the complexity of a shared cache pays for itself.

The speaker frames serving as a scheduling problem: requests, KV cache blocks, batching windows, and hardware memory all compete for the same resources.

The speaker highlights easy wins first: better batching, fewer copies, tighter tokenizers, and honest load tests before investing in exotic kernels.

Method and measurement. Each experiment reports hardware, batch sizes, prompt templates, and evaluation settings so the audience can judge how far the result will transfer. The methodology section walks through the baseline, the instrumentation used to measure it, and the conditions under which the improvement appears. The session includes a short live debugging segment in which a deliberately broken configuration is diagnosed from traces. Failure analysis is given as much time as the success story, including a list of assumptions that did not survive contact with real traffic.

Takeaways. The session ends with a short reading list and an invitation to contribute issues and reproduction scripts to the referenced project. Questions about scale were answered with a reminder that the operational envelope matters more than the peak headline number. The speaker recommends starting with the simplest configuration that satisfies the product requirement. The final advice is to document the assumptions behind a benchmark, because those assumptions are what future maintainers will question.

items.title: Speedrunning Retrieval-Augmented Chat
items.abstract:
Speedrunning Retrieval-Augmented Chat was recorded as a Lightning Talk session at the 2026 AI Engineering Summit. The session focuses on retrieval architectures, vector search, and persistent memory for knowledge work. The project referenced by this session is langchain-ai/langchain. The speaker combines architecture diagrams, production anecdotes, and benchmark results, and reserves time at the end for questions from practitioners.

The talk separates retrieval quality from memory quality: one is about finding evidence, the other about deciding what to keep and when to forget.

The speaker demonstrates why embedding model changes require full reindexing and how to stage such migrations without breaking production.

Memory services are evaluated on write amplification, retrieval precision, provenance, and the ability to delete user data safely.

Evaluation for retrieval is framed with recall at k, grounded answer rate, and citation quality, not only similarity scores.

The speaker closes with guidance on building retrieval APIs that agents can call repeatedly without flooding context windows.

Index design is covered in depth, including chunking, metadata filters, hybrid search, and reranking under tight latency budgets.

Failure analysis is given as much time as the success story, including a list of assumptions that did not survive contact with real traffic. The speaker explains how they decided which optimizations were worth maintaining and which were removed after the experiment.

Takeaways. The main takeaway is to measure the bottleneck before redesigning the architecture.
